detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the application of constitutionalism and constitutionalisation through the mechanism of judicial review in Bangladesh, India, and the United States. It examines how rule of law, separation of powers, and rights protection ground constitutionalism, while constitutionalisation reflects the evolution of constitutional norms under globalization, including international treaties and human rights. The paper traces Bangladesh's judiciary integrating international labor and environmental standards with frequent reference to Indian case law, contrasts India's balancing of international commitments with national jurisdiction in social justice jurisprudence, and analyzes the U.S. judiciary's cautious adoption of international norms under Originalist and Living Constitution approaches. It concludes by situating judicial review as a process for applying constitutional provisions to protect rights amid evolving global legal challenges.

title: Fintech Innovation, Short Selling, and Market Efficiency

detail.title: Fintech Innovation, Short Selling, and Market Efficiency

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper studies whether fintech innovation can relax short-sale constraints and improve price discovery. I examine Robinhood's May 2022 stock lending program, which mobilized dispersed retail shareholdings into the securities-lending market. Using a difference-indifferences design, I find evidence that the program relaxes short-sale constraints for stocks heavily owned by retail investors. Short interest rises by 0.43 percentage points among stocks more exposed to the program. Further evidence suggests that Robinhood helps bring retail-held shares into the lending market, increasing lendable supply outside the traditional institutional lending pool. I also find suggestive evidence of improved price discovery: anomaly-related pricing errors decline more among stocks exposed to the program, with larger declines on the short than on the long side for several anomalies. Overall, the evidence suggests that fintech innovation can relax limits to arbitrage and improve price discovery by making dispersed shareholdings easier to intermediate into the securities-lending market.

title: Factor Time

detail.title: Factor Time

detail.abstract: Factor models conventionally form portfolios annually using stale financial statements released months earlier. We construct fresh factors each month using the most recent annual financial statements. Fresh factors modestly improve pricing, but augmenting the stale model with the change in returns from updating stale portfolio assignments significantly improves pricing because the two components carry different pricing content. This reallocates abnormal returns, reverses the interpretation of thousands of event-study CARs, and reclassifies 14.7% of top-decile mutual funds. These findings reveal a fundamental structure in returns: a slow-moving component reflecting persistent fundamental risk and a fast-moving component capturing the arrival of information.

title: The Price and Platform of Entry: Rental Application Fees, Security Deposits, Digital Rent Payments, and Landlord Practices in U.S. Rental Housing

detail.title: The Price and Platform of Entry: Rental Application Fees, Security Deposits, Digital Rent Payments, and Landlord Practices in U.S. Rental Housing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is no conflict of interest and I'm the sole author

detail.abstract: Up-front rental charges and payment systems shape whether a household can enter and sustain a tenancy, yet national evidence rarely observes these practices together with the operating structure of the property. This paper uses the 2024 Rental Housing Finance Survey, a propertylevel probability sample representing 18,964,574 U.S. rental properties, to study application-fee bands, fee waivers, security-deposit requirements, and digital rent-payment options across owner-managed properties, directly employed management agents, and management companies. Weighted prevalence and linear-probability models use all 100 successive-difference replicate weights. Among properties with usable responses, 47.8% report an application fee of at least $50, 13.8% report a fee of $100 or more, 15.3% require more than one month's rent as a deposit, and 48.6% offer an online, mobile-app, card, or third-party payment option. After adjustment for property scale, ownership form, portfolio scale, asking rent, subsidy status, concessions, acquisition cohort, and configuration, management-company operation has the most stable exploratory association: a 24.2-percentage-point higher probability of digital payment than owner/self management (95% CI 4.6 to 43.8; p=0.016; BH q=0.188). Application-fee and deposit contrasts are less precise, and none of the twelve focal management contrasts survives Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment. The results therefore describe an uneven architecture of professionalization rather than confirmed causal effects. The paper contributes a reproducible national baseline among reporting properties for research on rental application fees, security deposits, digital rent payments, property management, landlord practices, tenant welfare, and housing affordability.

title:
Recursive Power-Plus Valuation: Martingale Feasibility and Viability Boundaries

Dedicated To the Memory of Our Friend Peter Carr, Whose Ideas Inspired This Work

detail.title:
Recursive Power-Plus Valuation: Martingale Feasibility and Viability Boundaries

Dedicated To the Memory of Our Friend Peter Carr, Whose Ideas Inspired This Work

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Power-plus valuation gives an elementary one-period option pricing formula and an explicit recursion under repeated application. We study when this algebraically prescribed recursion also admits a dynamically coherent multi-period martingale stopping representation. The key restriction is recursive. Whenever the holder continues at a successor state, that state must itself support the remaining prescribed recursion. 

For a stylized convertible claim, we solve this backward feasibility problem exactly. With n ≥ 2 future conversion dates, the viable states form the finite half-open interval D_n = [0, d_n), where d_n is the exact viability boundary. These boundaries contract strictly as the number of remaining conversion dates increases. Once finite exercise states disappear, recursive viability becomes strictly more restrictive than the ordinary one-step martingale bound. We construct finite-support Borel Markov kernels that realize the prescribed stopping values throughout the viable domains for each fixed contract. Finally, under dense conversion grids we identify a sharp phase transition. Depending on the relative scaling of the power parameter and the grid spacing, the issuance viability boundary either converges to a finite limit or diverges.

detail.abstract: Institutional investors commonly separate strategic asset allocation (SAA) from tactical asset allocation (TAA). This governance structure is practical, but repeated one-period tactical optimization can be dynamically suboptimal when positions persist, signals evolve, and changing exposure is costly. We develop a discrete-time benchmark-relative model with an evolving strategic reference, tactical return predictors, quadratic trading costs, and a discounted recursive entropic criterion for continuation-value uncertainty. The optimal policy trades partially toward a forward-looking dynamic aim portfolio. In a scalar benchmark, we derive an exact persistence threshold separating attenuation from amplification of current tactical signals relative to one-period TAA. In a transitory-predictor setting, greater uncertainty about future predictor realizations reduces the signal-driven aim but increases the adjustment rate toward it, lowering the net current signal response. We also characterize trading-cost effects, obtaining general multivariate value and action-penalty orderings and sharper directional policy results in scalar or aligned settings. We distinguish one-step action loss from the full recursive loss generated by repeatedly following a suboptimal policy, derive exact fixed-policy and policy-loss identities, and use them to choose the best rule within a restricted, governance-compatible two-step SAA-TAA family. Numerical illustrations show that value-based calibration can materially improve a simple institutional rule even when coefficient proximity to the dynamic optimum is a poor guide to economic performance.

detail.abstract: Why does relationship-based voice trade remain dominant in the U.S. corporate bond interdealer market despite lower-friction electronic alternatives, and is this market structure efficient? Using transaction-level data, we show that dealers increasingly choose voice venue when inventory imbalances make immediacy valuable, because voice venue provides access to established trading relationships. Voice execution is slower than electronic execution for micro trades but faster for orders of at least $100,000, which account for nearly all interdealer par volume. We develop and calibrate a searchand-matching model where dealers choose trading venues contingent on their inventory balances. Voice venue offers two advantages: on average dealers meet counterparties faster, and because dealers with large imbalances sort into the voice venue, they meet better counterparties, whose positions are more likely to offset their own. The endogenous second channel accounts for roughly three quarters of the voice venue's advantage in the calibrated model. In equilibrium, voice venues are valuable but inefficiently allocated and overused by dealers with limited need for immediacy. A social planner retains the most imbalanced dealers in voice but reallocates near-target dealers to electronic trading, reducing the share of dealers searching in voice from 72% to 25%.

detail.abstract: For an exogenous source of information and a prespecified number of messages k, I characterize the set of maximal--that is to say, undominated--summaries of the information that use at most k messages. When the exogenous information produces a regular distribution over posteriors (if it has a density on its affine hull, for instance), the maximal summaries take a precise geometric form. detail.abstract: We study a finite cyclic economy in which dealers hold an indivisible object and choose costly right and left directed search, being our starting point the dealers discounted control problem. Under an explicit sufficient profitability condition, a global bound on continuation values strictly fixes the signs of both directional incentives. Every stationary globally optimal policy is consequently vacancy-directed and bang-bang at holding states. The induced primitive transition channels then aggregate exactly to the generator of the periodic asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP), including the coincident-target multiplicity that arises on a two-site cycle. Thus, within the specified environment, the microscopic ASEP rates are implications of optimal behavior rather than primitive transition rules. We also give an exact local reduction of a dealer-search block taken from the over-the-counter search literature, construct an explicit family with smooth success and strictly convex cost primitives whose global maximizers converge to the relevant boundary effort away from a knife edge, and identify its limiting margin with a directional coefficient of the strategic model.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Financial Analytics: An Integrative Review of Financial Modeling, Forecasting, and Financial Controls
affiliations: East Texas A&M University and East Texas A&M University

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence in Financial Analytics: An Integrative Review of Financial Modeling, Forecasting, and Financial Controls
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) refers to computer systems designed to perform tasks that normally require human judgment. AI commonly helps recognize patterns, make predictions, and adapt to new information by continuously training models using concepts like machine learning, deep learning, and generative models. In finance, traditional, manual, and rule-based methods generate the data. Hence, AI can be a boon in the finance sector, with the ability to process large datasets regularly, catch anomalies and risks earlier, and turn raw data into insight-driven tools; there is more room for progress in the field. Moreover, AI has moved from a peripheral analytics tool to a core capability across corporate finance functions. [13] This report examines two applied pillars of AI in the financial system: modeling and prediction, and the use of AI for data controls. The first pillar is AI for financial modeling, using machine learning, natural language processing, and generative techniques to forecast revenue, cash flow, credit risk, and market behavior. The second pillar is AI for data controls, specifically using AI to automate reconciliation of financial data across multiple systems (bank feeds, sub-ledgers, general ledgers, and intercompany records) to strengthen controls over financial reporting. These two broader aspects can stand as discrete research, but they are also highly interdependent. Predictive financial models are only as reliable as the data they are trained and run on; in short, if the data that you train the model on is garbage, you are bound to get incorrect results from your data modeling tool. A classic concept of garbage in and garbage out (GIGO). Hence, data reliability is itself a function of how well an organization reconciles and governs a wide variety of, perhaps inconsistent, financial systems. This report argues that AI-driven reconciliation is not merely an efficiency initiative; it is an absolute necessity for reliable forecasting. This research focuses on the current state of AI in predictive modeling and controls, while highlighting risky areas like accuracy, transparency, data quality, and SOX controls. It also aims to provide a centralized solution to help companies use AI for both the forecasting and the control functions within finance.

detail.abstract: Why must a Cause of All and a Law of All be related in a universe? This paper tests that question as a hypothesis from the author's own research programme, the Architecture of Freedom Intelligence (AFI): that Freedom-the structured availability of possible continuation, called Passibility-is constitutive of causal production, and that this cause connects to a law of navigation, Lightness, through the open question of Navigability: how a system moves among the continuations open to it. Whether cause and law truly connect this way, or belong to separate registers entirely, is held open and tested against 52 independently verified 2025-2026 sources, forty counterfactual universes, and eight formal models. Key results: • Structured possibility generates a real navigation problem, but only under two contestable commitments: reality is compressible, and realization follows a single history.

detail.abstract: Entrepreneurial-exit research has established that exit is a consequential stage of the entrepreneurial process, yet scholarship and practice still devote more attention to routes, timing, and transaction outcomes than to the founder's post-liquidity decision environment. This conceptual paper integrates research on entrepreneurial exit, founder role identity, retirement adjustment, conservation of resources, recovery from work stress, affect and decision making, and adaptation to major life events. It develops the Exit Expedition model, which distinguishes ascent, summit, and descent as temporally different decision environments. Within descent, the paper introduces D.E.S.C.E.N.T. as a practicederived sequence of disruption, estrangement, separation, celebration, emptiness, noise, and transition; the Depletion Window as a hypothesized period of resource mismatch following liquidity; and the Six Centers of Doubt as a diagnostic map of self-image, relationships, work, health, prosperity, and significance. Seven propositions specify how identity centrality, resource change, emotional arousal, opportunity load, and decision reversibility may shape post-exit adjustment. The paper's primary contribution is a timing argument: the quality of a founder's post-exit choices may depend not only on what is decided, but on whether identity-defining and capital-intensive decisions are designed before, during, or after the role transition. Because the model is conceptual and practice-informed rather than empirically validated, a research agenda is offered for longitudinal and mixed-method testing.

title: Frictionless Losses: Deregulation, Exchange Incentives, and a Case for Platform-Level Risk Controls in Retail Options Markets

detail.title: Frictionless Losses: Deregulation, Exchange Incentives, and a Case for Platform-Level Risk Controls in Retail Options Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no financial relationship with any exchange, broker, or trading platform discussed in this paper. No funding was received for this research.
declarations.funderStatement: Unfunded. This research was conducted independently with no external financial support.

detail.abstract: In 2026, U.S. options markets went through three changes at roughly the same time: FINRA eliminated the Pattern Day Trader (PDT) rule and its $25,000 minimum-equity threshold (effective June 4, 2026); zero-daysto-expiration (0DTE) options kept growing, reaching a record 66.2% of S&P 500 index options volume by July; and Cboe completed a near-24-hour trading window covering SPX, VIX, Mini-SPX, and Russell 2000 index options. Using Cboe's own investor disclosures, this paper documents that all three changes are described to investors primarily in terms of engagement and volume growth, while retail-facing communications about the same events emphasize flexibility and access. This paper does not claim that any entity intended to harm retail traders, nor does it establish a causal link between these friction removals and retail trading losses. What it documents is an observable asymmetry in how the commercial value of these changes is communicated to different audiences. Combined with well-established findings that most retail options buyers lose money and that traders routinely fail to exit at planned loss levels, this asymmetry points to a gap in current disclosure regimes. The paper proposes a voluntary, opt-in risk control feature-a platform-level button, available inside any retail trading app, that traders can turn on or off at will-which, once activated, locks a trader's selfdefined loss threshold in place for a set period. Rooted in behavioral-economics commitment-device theory, it holds traders to their own stated risk plan at the moment when research predicts they are most likely to abandon it. AI is proposed as implementation infrastructure for this feature, not as the theoretical contribution.

publicationDetails.detailsText: SMU Centre for Digital Law Research Paper Forthcoming

detail.abstract: This Article examines how Singapore manages US pressure over semiconductor diversion without adopting US extraterritorial export-control logic. Taking AI-server diversion cases as its starting point, it contrasts a US regime that follows controlled items, end users, affiliates, and computing access across borders with Singapore’s territorial, list-based framework, anchored in the multilateral non-proliferation baseline beyond which US controls have moved. It introduces the ‘hub economy’ to explain that divergence: unlike chokepoint economies, asked to restrict what they produce, hub economies are asked to police what they host, handle, and route. Alignment turns on political judgment, not legal capacity: the Article argues that Singapore regards the costs to its strategic autonomy and hub standing as too high. It preserves ‘doctrinal independence’ by retaining multilateral categories and practices ‘doctrinal substitution’ by reaching diversion through general criminal law and, potentially, cybercrime law. Transactions through Singapore are constrained not by the regulatory divergence but by extraterritorial US controls, license conditions, and anticipatory firm compliance. Whether this balance holds remains open: remote-access controls, proposed legislation concerning chip traceability and corporate affiliation, and Pax Silica may narrow the space for non-alignment. The findings illuminate how States manage asymmetric extraterritorial pressure without converting it into domestic legal obligation.

title: Carbon Risk, Energy Security, and the Energy Transition: Cross-Country Evidence with Implications for Petro vs HID Economies

detail.title: Carbon Risk, Energy Security, and the Energy Transition: Cross-Country Evidence with Implications for Petro vs HID Economies

detail.abstract:
Purpose – This paper asks whether energy-transition margins can raise both productivity and energy security at once, whether the answer depends on a country's position as a net energy exporter or an import-dependent economy, and whether any resulting risk is priced by financial markets.

Design/methodology/approach – Using an unbalanced panel of up to 207 countries, the paper estimates an augmented STIRPAT/Cobb–Douglas model with country and year fixed effects, then extends a double-index asset-pricing model with a third, orthogonalized energy-security risk factor, testing whether the resulting country-level loading is priced into sovereign risk premia and realized growth across rolling estimation windows (2009–2023).

Findings – Energy-exporting and import-dependent economies draw productivity from different energy margins (energy intensity versus emission intensity, respectively). Systematic carbon risk is significantly priced into country risk premia, but systematic energy-security risk is not; its association with growth is significant only in windows overlapping major energy-geopolitical shocks.

Originality/value – This is the first study to test the producer/consumer energy-security asymmetry jointly in a growth-panel and a three-factor asset-pricing framework, and to document its time-varying, event-driven pricing pattern.

Practical implications – Energy-transition policy should be differentiated by a country's position in global energy trade: Petro (net-exporter) and HID (import-dependent) economies draw productivity from different energy margins, so sovereign risk pricing cannot rely on a single global metric for both.

detail.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (Generative AI) gradually permeates the core operations of firms as a general-purpose technology (GPT), a pronounced empirical gap has emerged between its outstanding performance at the micro-task level and the lagged productivity data observed at the macroeconomic and firm levels. While a substantial body of micro-experimental evidence consistently demonstrates that generative AI can substantively improve both the speed and quality of specific cognitive tasks, this technological enthusiasm has not immediately translated into commensurate net productivity gains when the analytical lens is elevated to overall firm performance. This paper aims to open the black box between "task efficiency" and "firm valuation," examining the organizational frictions and temporal lags that mediate the relationships among technological exposure, substantive adoption, and net economic returns. By constructing firm-level panel data and employing an event-study framework, the paper not only explains why short-term financial metrics struggle to capture the full economic impact of AI, but also investigates how capital markets prospectively reprice firms on the basis of expected future cash flows. Our findings indicate that understanding the economic consequences of generative AI requires treating it as a friction-laden process of organizational reconfiguration rather than a simple exogenous technological shock.

detail.abstract: This paper aims to answer the question "To what extent is ExxonMobil's acquisition of Pioneer Natural Resources increasing its operational efficiency?" Key findings show that ExxonMobil's acquisition of Pioneer is one that generates significant operational efficiency. An increase in both capital productivity and labour productivity highlight that the business is able to produce more barrels of oil per dollar of capital input and per employee, with increases of around 14% and 16% respectively. However, overtime, it is unclear whether the extent of operational efficiency may be enough to achieve their objective in generating double digit returns.

title: The Bolivian Paradox: A Negotiauction Framework for Sovereign Lithium Monetisation

detail.title: The Bolivian Paradox: A Negotiauction Framework for Sovereign Lithium Monetisation

detail.abstract: Bolivia possesses approximately 22% of identified global lithium resources-one of the world's largest endowments-yet in 2025 produced just 2,400 tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent, less than 1% of South American output. This paper demonstrates that Bolivia's production gap is primarily institutional: a bilateral monopoly with Chinese and Russian state-owned enterprises has trapped the sovereign in a low-BATNA equilibrium, enabling counterparties to capture quasi-rents through opaque pricing and one-sided risk allocation. We propose Commodity-Linked Participation Rights (CLPRs), an exchange-cleared security that transforms Bolivia's bargaining structure from bilateral negotiation to a "negotiauction"-a hybrid mechanism in which competitive bidding determines price while negotiated governance provisions preserve sovereign discretion. Drawing on Subramanian's negotiauction theory and Acemoglu and Robinson's institutional economics framework, we develop a formal bargaining model in which the credible availability of a CLPR auction improves the sovereign's outside option, altering the equilibrium terms of bilateral resource negotiations. Under our baseline parameterisation, the simulated effective financing cost falls from an implicit 12%+ to approximately 7.4%, with the probability of payment distress declining from 35% to 8.2%. The framework generalises to other resource-rich developing economies facing sovereignty-financing trade-offs.

detail.title: The Case for Mandatory AI Ethics Audits in Government Utilization

detail.abstract:
This white paper argues that the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence in government decision‑making has outpaced the constitutional, philosophical, and democratic safeguards required to ensure accountability. Drawing on forty‑five years of legal practice and direct experience with clients harmed by opaque algorithmic systems, the paper contends that government use of AI without meaningful transparency, explanation, or appeal rights is not merely poor policy—it is constitutionally suspect under the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments. When citizens receive a code instead of an explanation, due process becomes a fiction.

The paper situates this concern within a long Western tradition of political philosophy. From Plato’s requirement that rulers “give an account,” to Aquinas’s insistence that law must serve the common good and respect human dignity, to Leo XIII’s principle of subsidiarity, to Will Rogers’s plainspoken demand that government remain understandable to ordinary Americans, the argument converges on a single truth: power exercised over persons must remain accountable to those persons. Algorithmic governance, when opaque, violates that tradition.

The paper further demonstrates that the accountability gap is not partisan. Conservatives wary of bureaucratic overreach and progressives focused on algorithmic discrimination share a common interest in ensuring that AI systems do not operate beyond public scrutiny. Mandatory ethics audits—independent, transparent, and enforceable—offer a practical, bipartisan path forward.

To operationalize this, the paper proposes a federal Office of AI Ethics Accountability, an independent AI Ethics Audit Corps, and a public registry of audit findings. These structures would embed transparency, fairness testing, human responsibility, and meaningful redress into every government AI system. The governing principle—Keep the Humane in the Loop—is presented not as sentiment but as a constitutional requirement. The paper concludes that America has repeatedly risen to similar governance challenges and can do so again, provided it acts before algorithmic systems become too entrenched to reform.

detail.abstract: This study examines the effect of behavioral biases and the moderating effect of financial literacy on financial performance of SMEs in Afghanistan. This study adopted quantitative research design and primary data were collected from 300 SMEs in three provinces of Afghanistan namely Nangarhar, Helmand and Khost through structured questionnaire. The study employed exploratory factor analysis (EFA), correlation analysis, multiple regression and hierarchical regression to establish the effect of biases on the financial performance of SMEs. The study results indicated that overconfidence bias has a significant positive relationship with the financial performance of SMEs while the anchoring effect bias, herding behavior bias and the loss aversion has a significant negative relationship with the financial performance of SMEs. Among these, loss aversion was most strongly related to financial performance. The regression result also suggested that financial literacy has a significant impact in reducing the relationship between behavioral biases and financial performance. That is, it reduces the negative impact of behavioral biases. This study is one of the first to apply the concepts of behavioral finance to a fragile post-conflict setting and offers some suggestions for policy makers, financial institutions and business owners to improve the performance of SMEs by enhancing the financial literacy and awareness of their stakeholders.

title: From Overconfidence to Overfitting: Bias Substitution, Model Monoculture and a Measurement Agenda for Indian Markets

detail.abstract: Behavioural finance has spent decades establishing that individual investors are predictably irrational and has generally treated the resulting errors as noise: costly to the individual, but largely diversifiable in aggregate. This article argues that the diffusion of generative artificial intelligence among Indian retail investors will quietly withdraw that assumption. Conversational models do not so much remove bias from decision-making as substitute one class of bias for another — smaller in magnitude for each participant, and considerably more correlated across participants. For the individual trader, the exchange may well be favourable. Regarding market structure, it may be a more hazardous arrangement and is not currently measured. The article proceeds in three steps. First, it sets out a taxonomy in which eight familiar behavioural biases are mapped onto their algorithmic successors, arguing that the fluency– calibration gap, sycophantic accommodation and training-corpus coverage skew carry most of the analytical weight. Second, it traces the path by which correlated error at the level of individual reasoning becomes a market-structure problem, drawing on the literature on algorithmic monoculture, foundation-model homogenisation and overlapping-portfolio contagion, and identifies four features of the Indian market — the scale of retail derivatives participation, concentration in the intermediation layer, thin free float in the small-cap and SME segments, and the formalisation of retail algorithmic access — that sharpen the mechanism. Third, it examines the regulatory position, noting that the accountability architecture assembled by the Securities and Exchange Board of India operates almost entirely at the level of the individual entity, whereas monoculture is a system-level property that no entity can observe from within its own perimeter. The article concludes with a suggestion on measurement. Retail algorithmic strategies are registered with and approved by a recognised stock exchange. The resulting orders carry unique identifiers, and Indian exchanges are accumulating a near-complete registry of the automated strategies linkable to the order flow they generate. Four measures are proposed on that foundation. Three of them — a strategy similarity index, model provenance disclosure, and realised co-movement of registered strategies — draw on data the exchanges already hold. The fourth, a standing prompt–response audit, requires no regulatory access whatever. The convergence described here has not been established; it is put forward as a claim to be tested, and the agenda is designed to be cheap to falsify.

declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: In our previous study, ECB Interest Rate Forecasting under High Inflation Pressures, we introduced a linear forecasting model for euro-area policy rates based on the EURIBOR term structure. The model successfully approximated changes in the ECB main refinancing operations rate during the 2022-2023 monetary tightening cycle. Drawing on evidence from recent ECB tightening episodes, we identified a more precise estimate of the trigger variable associated with the onset of monetary tightening, improving the empirical specification and applicability of the forecasting framework. The model also incorporates a rounding rule to the nearest 5 basis points, reflecting the discrete nature of ECB policy-rate decisions and aligning forecast values with the increments typically observed in monetary policy adjustments. Overall, the refined specification improves the predictive performance of the model and enhances its ability to anticipate future ECB policy decisions during periods of elevated inflationary pressures (JEL Code: E52).

title: Household Influence in the Stock Market: A Belief-Based Approach *
affiliations: ,  and Tilburg University

detail.title: Household Influence in the Stock Market: A Belief-Based Approach *

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare
declarations.funderStatement: Nothing to declare

detail.abstract: A frictionless view holds that intermediaries do not affect asset prices because households alone determine valuations. A simple model of delegation shows instead that prices reflect a weighted average of households' and intermediaries' subjective beliefs, with household influence determined by delegation strength, risk attitudes, and intermediaries' regulatory and contractual incentives. We use investor surveys to recover household influence as a time-varying latent process. We reject the frictionless view even in the stock market, arguably the least intermediated major asset class, while showing that the growth of intermediation substantially overstates the dilution of household influence. We link fluctuations in influence to risk, financial constraints, and the regulatory and technological forces reshaping US markets.

title: The Hidden Costs of Trade Protection: Agency Problems in Firms Shielded from Competition
affiliations: Colorado State University, Fort Collins - Department of Finance & Real Estate and

detail.title: The Hidden Costs of Trade Protection: Agency Problems in Firms Shielded from Competition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We have no declaration of interest to report.
declarations.funderStatement: We have no funder statement to report.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how trade protection shapes firm investment and governance. Using the U.S.-China trade war as a setting, we find that firms shielded from import competition raise R&D spending while the value of their innovation falls. The same firms cut equity issuance and raise leverage, avoiding the scrutiny that comes with outside financing, and their CEOs' equity incentives decline. Managers spend more and create less, a pattern that points to agency costs rather than the quiet life. The results highlight the governance costs of shielding firms from foreign competition.

title: Advanced Manufacturing Technologies: A Comprehensive Review of Smart Manufacturing, Robotics, Additive Manufacturing, AI, and Digital Twins

detail.title: Advanced Manufacturing Technologies: A Comprehensive Review of Smart Manufacturing, Robotics, Additive Manufacturing, AI, and Digital Twins

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable (no human or animal subjects).
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this study.

detail.abstract: Advanced manufacturing encompasses integrated technologies like IoT, robotics, 3D printing, AI, and digital twins to create smart factories with higher productivity, quality, and customization. We review recent peer-reviewed and industry sources to assess technology categories, performance metrics, and case studies. A systematic literature search (IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Google Scholar, standards bodies) identified trends and data on productivity, cost, quality, lead times, and energy impacts. Key findings: IoT/AI and robotics can reduce downtime 30–50% and improve throughput 10–30%; smart sensors and predictive maintenance cut defects and costs by up to 70% in case studies; additive manufacturing is highly beneficial for complex parts and small runs; digital twins yield 20–30% cost savings in simulations. Tables summarize technology taxonomy, performance gains, and standards. Figures illustrate manufacturing systems and process flows. We discuss implications for supply chains, workforce, and sustainability. Quantitative metrics are drawn from literature; where data was lacking we note assumptions. The paper concludes with future research directions on standards, metrics, and integrated platforms.

title: Algorithmic Tax Ownership
affiliations: Yeshiva University - Benjamin N. Cardozo School of Law and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Algorithmic Tax Ownership

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

publicationDetails.detailsText: 51 BYU L. Rev. 1437 (2026)

detail.abstract:
Tax ownership is a crucial concept for determining tax liabilities, compliance, and enforcement. However, neither the courts nor the IRS has provided clear guidance on how to analyze it. Since the Supreme Court first outlined a twenty-six-factor test for determining tax ownership in Frank Lyon Co. v. United States in 1978, this multifactor test has remained largely unchanged, and there has been no further guidance from the courts or the IRS to this day. Even tests with shorter lists of factors only add to the confusion regarding compliance and enforcement, as there is no clarity on which factors are most dispositive.

This Article provides a better understanding of tax ownership analysis by addressing this question with machine learning algorithms. After analyzing 2,000 IRS rulings and court cases related to sale and repurchase transactions, this Article’s algorithmic model found that a single factor of identifying who bears the economic benefits and burdens of the underlying asset can predict a tax ownership outcome with 94.6% accuracy. Additionally, this Article demonstrates how the proposed model and its findings could be applied to other types of transactions, providing various stakeholders with an advanced tool to assess and refine their decisions without overhauling existing substantive case law.

This Article’s analysis of multi-factors in tax ownership may resonate with broader audiences who are studying multifactor tests in another area of law. Also, the comparison of the proposed algorithm using classic machine learning with regression, natural language processing, and large language models would inspire legal scholars exploring cutting-edge methodologies.

title: Artificial Intelligence in International Supply Chain Management: Evidence From a Global Consumer Goods Company
affiliations: MGIMO University

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence in International Supply Chain Management: Evidence From a Global Consumer Goods Company

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are reshaping business process management within international supply chains, using the operations of a major multinational fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) company as an illustrative case. Drawing on a synthesis of the author's master's research and publicly available corporate and industry sources, the paper systematizes the principal areas of AI application in supply chain management-demand forecasting, inventory optimization, computer vision-based quality control, and predictive logistics analytics-and evaluates their contribution to operational efficiency. The analysis indicates that AI-enabled predictive tools support a shift from reactive to anticipatory supply chain management, yet their effectiveness remains constrained by data heterogeneity across international suppliers and by the scale of investment required for enterprise-wide deployment. The paper concludes that sustainable gains from AI adoption in global supply chains depend on complementary organizational measures, including data standardization and continued human oversight of algorithmic recommendations.

title: Investing in Artificial Intelligence: From the Chip to the Application -How Investors Can Take Part in the Second Megatrend

detail.title: Investing in Artificial Intelligence: From the Chip to the Application -How Investors Can Take Part in the Second Megatrend

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No one influenced this study
declarations.funderStatement: No funder

detail.abstract: No technology has ever moved so much capital in so little time: the four large cloud groups plan to invest around USD 735 billion in 2026 — more than five times their 2023 outlay —, NVIDIA's data-centre business approaches USD 200 billion in annual revenue, and the model providers OpenAI and Anthropic report annualised revenues of more than 40 and 65 billion US dollars respectively. This paper — the second of six on the great megatrends — classifies artificial intelligence as a general purpose technology, maps its value chain from chips through data centres and models to applications, and tests the bubble question against hard numbers. The empirical picture cuts both ways. On the one hand, controlled studies document sizeable productivity gains — 15 per cent in customer service, 40 per cent time saved in writing tasks, 56 per cent faster programming — and the investments are largely paid out of the current profits of the world's most profitable companies. On the other hand, index concentration has reached historic highs — the ten largest US names make up more than 40 per cent of the S&P 500, more than at the peak of the dotcom bubble —, circular financing between chip makers, cloud providers and model firms is growing, and according to a widely discussed MIT study 95 per cent of corporate pilot projects have yet to deliver a measurable profit contribution. For investors, the paper names listed companies along the entire chain — exclusively large and mid caps, with business idea and trading venues — and applies the fixed ETF checklist: physical replication, fund size of at least EUR 0.2 billion, sustainability classification, costs, the currency question, issuer, UCITS framework and exchange trading. The most important single lesson: whoever holds a world index already owns roughly a third of the AI complex through its heavyweights — every additional position is a deliberate overweight and should be sized accordingly.

title: The 2026 Draft EU Merger Guidelines: Continuity, Refinement and Recalibration of the EUMR Framework

detail.title: The 2026 Draft EU Merger Guidelines: Continuity, Refinement and Recalibration of the EUMR Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract: This article examines the draft Guidelines published by the European Commission on 30 April 2026 for the interpretation and enforcement of Council Regulation (EC) No 139/2004 on the control of concentrations between undertakings (EUMR). While the draft Guidelines introduce significant developments in merger assessment, they do not constitute a departure from the framework that has guided EU merger control since the 2004 reform. Rather, they reflect the result of a process of continuity, refinement and recalibration aimed at adapting the EUMR framework to the changing conditions of contemporary societies. Against this background, the article analyses the enhanced role attributed to non-price parameters of competition, digital market characteristics, sustainability considerations and labour-market effects, alongside the strengthening of evidentiary standards and procedural discipline within the Significant Impediment to Effective Competition test. It further examines the extent to which the draft Guidelines clarify the institutional architecture of EU merger control, particularly in relation to the allocation of responsibilities between the Commission and the Member States under Article 21 EUMR. This contribution argues that, rather than altering the foundations of the post-2004 merger control regime, the draft Guidelines systematise and operationalise developments already emerging from the Commission’s decisional practice, the case law of the EU Courts and broader policy debates concerning the future direction of competition law.

title: Investing in Urbanisation: From the Apartment to the Water Network -How Investors Can Take Part in the Third Megatrend

detail.title: Investing in Urbanisation: From the Apartment to the Water Network -How Investors Can Take Part in the Third Megatrend

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No one influenced this study
declarations.funderStatement: No funder

detail.abstract: By 2050, the United Nations projects that just over two-thirds of the world's population will live in cities — with almost one billion urban dwellers added along the way. At the same time, the UN changed its counting method in 2025 and thereby redrew the map of the world's cities: under the new, satellite-based delineation, the largest city in the world is no longer Tokyo but Jakarta. This paper — the third of six on the great megatrends — places urbanisation in its economic context: from the agglomeration advantages that make cities more productive than their hinterland, through the housing shortage of the rich world, to the infrastructure gap that consultancies put at more than 100 trillion US dollars through 2040. The paper covers six fields of action of the megatrend: densification and intelligent housing, the green and resilient city, smart cities and digital connectivity, new urban mobility, the demographic change of the ageing city, and the tension between growing metropolises and shrinking regions. Empirically, a twofold picture emerges: the large cities of the rich world face historic scarcity — Germany alone is short of roughly 1.4 million homes and vacancy in its metropolises is close to zero — while at the same time half of Europe's municipalities are shrinking and a third of the world's shrinking cities are in China. For investors, the paper translates the megatrend into listed companies along the entire urban value chain — exclusively large- and mid-cap names, each with its business idea and trading venues — and into an ETF selection based on a fixed checklist: physical replication, fund volume of at least 0.2 billion euros, costs, the currency question, issuer, UCITS status and exchange tradability. One central finding: an ETF that covers the megatrend of urbanisation as a whole does not yet exist in Europe — investors have to assemble it themselves from infrastructure, water, real estate and smart city funds.

title: International Comparison of Healthcare Structures Using Principal Component Analysis: Characteristics and Policy Implications of Japan's High-Intensity, Low-Physician-Input Healthcare Structure
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: International Comparison of Healthcare Structures Using Principal Component Analysis: Characteristics and Policy Implications of Japan's High-Intensity, Low-Physician-Input Healthcare Structure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This study was conducted independently and is not connected to the author’s professional duties. All analyses, interpretations, and conclusions represent the author’s personal academic work and do not reflect the views of any organization.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not require ethics approval. The analysis is based exclusively on publicly available, aggregate-level data from the OECD and other official statistical sources. No individual-level, confidential, or personally identifiable information was used.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no financial support. The author did not receive funding, grants, or institutional assistance from any public or private organization. All work was conducted independently using the author’s own resources.

detail.abstract:
This study applies principal component analysis (PCA) to healthcare structures in 27 countries, primarily OECD members, and examines the characteristics of Japan's healthcare structure and their policy implications.
The analysis identifies four principal components: Healthcare Intensity, Public Financing Intensity, Cost-Sharing Intensity (Pharmaceutical-Centered), and Physician Input Intensity.
Japan is characterized by exceptionally high Healthcare Intensity, reflected in long hospital stays, abundant hospital beds, frequent physician consultations, and extensive CT scanner availability, while exhibiting relatively low Physician Input Intensity.
As population aging progresses, this healthcare structure may increase upward pressure on healthcare expenditure by translating rising healthcare needs into greater healthcare utilization.
The findings suggest that healthcare reform in Japan should focus on reducing Healthcare Intensity while maintaining Public Financing Intensity and increasing Physician Input Intensity, with gatekeeper systems and prospective payment systems (DRG/PPS) representing potentially useful policy instruments.

title: Continuous-Time Phase-Conditioned Predictive-Directional Association

detail.title: Continuous-Time Phase-Conditioned Predictive-Directional Association

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts
declarations.ethicsApproval: No Ethics approval is required..
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded
declarations.clinicalTrialRegistration: No Clinical trial registration is required.

detail.abstract: The general Predictive-Directional Association (PDA) functional quantifies directed association via total-variation distance between conditional distributions, without requiring stationarity or parametric assumptions. Existing temporal specializations operate in discrete time and produce a single scalar summary over the observation window. In oscillatory systems, however, directed influences may be localized to specific phases of the cycle, and a global scalar can obscure such phase-specific structure. This paper develops the continuous-time, phase-conditioned extension of temporal PDA. For a stochastic process with a phase variable on the circle, we define a phase-resolved PDA profile over the oscillation cycle, replacing a single scalar with a function of phase. The definition is purely probabilistic and requires no Gaussianity, linearity, or stationarity of the unconditional process. We also introduce a finite-history truncation which, for fixed time, exactly recovers the full-history object when the truncation window covers the entire past. An estimation framework for the finite-history object is outlined under finite-state binning and oracle-phase assumptions. The phase-conditioned PDA is positioned as a third distinct conditioning/temporalresolution dimension of the general PDA framework, complementing the existing time-delay and event-predictive branches. It is a distributional measure of directed predictive association and is not claimed to be equivalent to Granger causality.

title: When Do fastdid and Stata csdid Agree? A Replication and Practitioner's Checklist

detail.title: When Do fastdid and Stata csdid Agree? A Replication and Practitioner's Checklist

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. The views expressed in this paper are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the official position of the Ministry of Industry and Technology of the Republic of Türkiye.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses anonymised administrative firm-level data and does not involve human participants.

detail.abstract: The Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) estimator for staggered treatment adoption is now available in several software packages, and applied researchers increasingly rely on the assumption that these implementations, sharing a common theoretical foundation, will return the same answer from the same data. This paper examines that assumption directly by comparing the `fastdid` package in R with the `csdid` package in Stata on a placebo design in which the true treatment effect is known to be zero by construction. We draw a broad, treatment-free sample of one hundred thousand Turkish firms, assign a fake staggered adoption year at random, and estimate the overall effect in both packages. The central finding is reassuring rather than alarming: when five specific settings are aligned across the two tools, they agree to six decimal places, and both sit at the placebo zero. The risks we do identify lie elsewhere than in dramatic silent divergence. The most consequential is a trap in the shape of the output itself: one package's compact result contains two rows, a pre-trend diagnostic and the actual treatment effect, and reading the wrong row silently reports a pre-trend as if it were the estimate, with no warning. We began this study expecting to document large hidden discrepancies between the two implementations. The evidence pointed instead to a more useful conclusion, which we state as a short checklist: the tools are trustworthy when settings are aligned, and the practitioner's real task is to read the right quantity and to report which settings were matched.

detail.abstract: Autonomous software agents that hold funds and transact without human intervention moved into production between 2025 and 2026, on rails governed by major standards bodies and backed by the payments establishment. The assurance discipline that would let a regulated institution trust, examine, or answer for such an agent has not arrived with them. This paper locates the gap precisely — unverifiable counterparty software, unstandardized delegation of authority, and audit records that establish occurrence but not legitimacy — and argues that the missing methodology already exists in safety‑critical systems engineering. It presents an Agentic Finance Assurance Framework translating that discipline into five elements(verifiabledelegation, policy as enforceable constraint, consequence‑graded assurance cases, runtime invariants with mandated halt semantics, and provenance‑grade audit), a minimal graph‑native reference model that makes the framework’s central questions answer able by query, a worked example from a production autonomous trading system operated by the author,and a five‑rung adoption path that dock sin to the model‑risk, third party‑risk, and audit programs institutions already run. The framework is protocol agnostic by design: the rails will churn; the questions an examiner asks will not.

title: Macroeconomic Adjustment under Sanctions, Monetary Expansion, and Exchange-Rate Pressure: A Descriptive and Econometric Analysis of Iran

detail.title: Macroeconomic Adjustment under Sanctions, Monetary Expansion, and Exchange-Rate Pressure: A Descriptive and Econometric Analysis of Iran

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants, patients, animals, or personally identifiable data.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this working paper.

detail.abstract: This paper combines descriptive evidence with annual and quarterly econometric analysis of Iran's macroeconomic adjustment, focusing on exports, inflation, liquidity, exchange-rate dynamics, real interest rates, and sanctions-related regime shifts. The principal empirical contribution is a reconstructed quarterly free-market USD/IRR dataset for 2012Q1-2024Q2 based on TGJU market observations, combined with IMF International Financial Statistics quarterly goods exports. To distinguish the immediate exchange-rate shock surrounding the May 2018 U.S. withdrawal from the JCPOA from subsequent dynamics, the preferred quarterly specification separates an event-quarter indicator for 2018Q2 from a post-2018Q3 regime indicator. The event quarter is associated with an exceptionally large exchange-rate adjustment, while the sustained post-2018Q3 regime is not statistically significant in the mean-depreciation regression. By contrast, the post-2018Q3 regime is associated with roughly 9.2 percentage points of additional absolute quarterly exchange-rate change, conditional on goods-export growth and the earlier sanctions regime, with Newey-West HAC inference significant at the 1% level. A Pesaran-Shin-Smith bounds test does not support a stable longrun cointegrating relation between the exchange-rate level and goods exports, so no long-run export elasticity is reported. The evidence therefore supports a cautious conclusion: the post-2018 period is more robustly associated with elevated free-market exchange-rate instability than with a constant increase in mean quarterly depreciation.

title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Sieve Networks for High-Dimensional Estimation and Inference

detail.title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Sieve Networks for High-Dimensional Estimation and Inference

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Declarations of interest: none.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by a Toronto Metropolitan University Graduate Fellowship.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces Kolmogorov-Arnold Sieve Networks (KASNs), a novel deep learning framework for nonparametric estimation and semiparametric inference in high-dimensional settings. By integrating the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem into a sieve extremum framework and leveraging sparsity, our proposed method achieves an explicit asymptotic rate of convergence in the root-mean-square norm of o_{P}(n^{-1/4}). The sparse compositional structure imposed on the target function embeds multipleindex and latent factor models, capturing nonlinear interactions across covariates while preserving dimension-free convergence rates. This framework delivers asymptotically normal plug-in estimators and facilitates nuisance function estimation within Double/Debiased Machine Learning (DML). These are areas where existing deep neural network architectures are less suited due to their black box nature, reliance on i.i.d. assumptions, and slower convergence rates. KASNs overcome these limitations through a learnable B-spline activation function structure that is theoretically compatible with stationary mixing processes.

title: Rethinking Predictability: Distributional Forecasts of the Market Risk Premium
affiliations: Bradley University - Department of Finance

detail.title: Rethinking Predictability: Distributional Forecasts of the Market Risk Premium

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no personal or financial relationships with other people or organizations that could have inappropriately influenced, or reasonably be perceived to have influenced, this research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Market risk premium forecasts are traditionally evaluated through point forecasts of expected returns, implicitly treating the conditional expectation as a sufficient representation of future uncertainty. This paper examines whether evaluating predictive distributions alongside point forecasts provides additional information for portfolio allocation and risk management. Predictive distributions are generated using a simulation-based geometric Brownian motion framework and evaluated using both statistical and economic criteria. Consistent with the return predictability literature, the conditional expectation exhibits limited forecasting power. The predictive distributions, however, are reasonably well calibrated and satisfy several standard density forecast evaluation criteria. Portfolio analyses indicate that while expectation-based strategies generate the highest terminal wealth and strongest conventional risk-adjusted performance, distribution-based strategies substantially reduce volatility, drawdowns, and tail-risk exposure. The results suggest that forecasting models should be evaluated not only by the accuracy of their point forecasts, but also by how effectively they characterize the uncertainty surrounding future outcomes.

title: It's time to Retire the Wharton Index
affiliations: Land Use Atlas, Inc.,  and Land Use Atlas, Inc.

detail.title: It's time to Retire the Wharton Index

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have contributed to the construction of the National Zoning Atlas and all are affiliated with Land Use Labs, which provided the data used in the analysis.
declarations.funderStatement: The authors received no financial support for the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.

detail.abstract: Empirical research on land use regulation has a credibility problem. For two decades, studies linking regulation to housing costs, residential segregation, and social mobility have primarily relied on an unreliable metric: the Wharton Residential Land Use Regulatory Index (WRLURI). Developed from surveys of local governments across the United States in 2005 and 2018, the Wharton Index claims to quantify the restrictiveness of regulation at the municipal and metropolitan level in a single number. Cited over 1,500 times in academic research and used widely in policy reports and government studies, its survey-based outcomes have never been fully scrutinized, nor have they been tested against actual land use regulations on the ground. In this paper, we audit the Wharton Index. We first disassemble its twelve subindices to clarify how they are made, finding that they have little to do with the content of any regulations at all. We then map its coverage, showing that its metropolitan-area-level scores rest on thin, unrepresentative slices of the regions they are used to rank. Finally, we assess the 2018 index against standardized zoning data from the National Zoning Atlas, measuring not just whether regulations exist but how much land they govern. The associations between WRLURI scores and actually existing restrictive zoning rules are essentially random, if not negative. These findings call for a full reassessment of the scholarship built from the index and of the wider body of knowledge that work appears to have settled. It is time to retire the Wharton Index.

detail.abstract: Differentiated tax regimes assume that a class of firms can be identified in advance and that membership predicts the constraint the policy is meant to relieve. This paper tests that premise on 67,899 firm-year observations of Italian certified innovative start-ups, innovative SMEs and ordinary small firms between 2014 and 2025. One effective-tax-rate equation is estimated three times: across five panel estimators, inside an unsupervised partition of the same firms, and against thirteen learning algorithms fitted to the same observations. Capitalisation and public contributions dominate, carrying seventy per cent of outof-sample predictive content, while the spread across the three registers is three points against seven for firm size alone, whose gradient is non-monotone. The partition rejects a common coefficient vector in twenty of twenty-one comparisons: the equity coefficient varies twelvefold and vanishes among grantfunded firms. Fiscal relief keyed to balance-sheet behaviour reaches this population more evenly than relief keyed to certification.

title: Standardization Governance and Urban Green Innovation: Transmission Mechanisms and Spatial Spillovers for Sustainable Cities
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN and Qingdao University

detail.title: Standardization Governance and Urban Green Innovation: Transmission Mechanisms and Spatial Spillovers for Sustainable Cities

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper
declarations.funderStatement: This study was supported by the Humanities and Social Sciences Youth Foundation, Ministry of Education (CN) (No. 22YJCZH234), and the Natural Science Foundation Project of Shandong Province (CN) (No. ZR202211140071)

detail.abstract: Standardization governance profoundly reshapes environmental innovation by driving institutional interoperability, knowledge codification, and voluntary compliance. Exploiting China ' s National Standardization Reform Pilot (NSRP) as a quasi-natural experiment, we leverage a staggered difference-indifferences (DID) design across 278 cities (2012-2022) to evaluate its causal impact on urban green innovation (UGI). Baseline estimates demonstrate that this institutional reform significantly catalyzes UGI, yielding magnified dividends in jurisdictions characterized by advanced economic development, elevated standardization priority, stringent environmental oversight, and quality-oriented governance. Transmission mechanisms reveals that standardization accelerates UGI primarily by optimizing resource allocation efficiency-a pathway robustly moderated by intellectual property protection-while simultaneously fostering talent agglomeration and activating regional technology markets. Crucially, estimations across multiple spatial matrices, complemented by dynamic distance profiles, uncover robust spatial spillovers of NSRPinduced UGI across geographic proximity, economic association, transport association, and joint green technology linkages. Although peaking within immediate physical proximities, these environmental dividends decisively reject a uniform spatial decay pattern; they also propagate through economic and transport networks, reaching geographically distant but functionally interconnected policy hubs. Ultimately, these findings illuminate the vital role of harmonized institutional frameworks in dismantling cross-jurisdictional frictions, accelerating regional knowledge diffusion, and driving sustainable urban transitions.

title: Who is Watching? Gender Composition of Observers and Risk Taking
affiliations: ,  and New York University (NYU) - New York University, Abu Dhabi

detail.title: Who is Watching? Gender Composition of Observers and Risk Taking

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: NYU Abu Dhabi, Experimental Social Science Laboratory

detail.abstract: We experimentally investigate whether the gender composition of an observing peer group affects individual risk-taking. Participants are randomly assigned to three-person groups differing only in gender composition. They complete an incentivized lottery task knowing that their choices will be observed by the other group members. We find that men's willingness to choose the riskiest lottery increases monotonically with the number of female observers, whereas women exhibit no comparable response to the number of male observers. Men in all-male groups display levels of risk-taking statistically indistinguishable from those of women in all-female groups, indicating that the observed gender gap emerges primarily in mixed-gender groups. A mating-motivated signaling mechanism is consistent with our results.

title: Quiet Before the Storm: Dynamic Ensemble Learning beyond Sparsity
affiliations: , University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) - Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science (AMSS) and Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) - Center for Forecasting Science; Academy of Mathematics and Systems Sciences

detail.title: Quiet Before the Storm: Dynamic Ensemble Learning beyond Sparsity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: Forecasting macroeconomic and financial variables under structural changes increasingly relies on a large pool of predictors,  raising a fundamental question: should one impose sparsity, selecting a few key drivers, or density, pooling information across many? This paper develops a dynamic ensemble learning (DEL) framework that addresses this challenge by adaptively combining sparse and dense models through data-driven and time-varying combination weights, without committing to either structure ex ante. We establish the asymptotic optimality of the DEL estimator and the consistency of the combination weights for out-of-sample prediction, even when all candidate models are misspecified. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through extensive simulations and an application to U.S. inflation forecasting. Empirically, neither the sparse nor the dense specification dominates uniformly. By adapting to changes in their relative performance, DEL reduces forecast error by more than 16% relative to either constituent model. These improvements in predictive accuracy are accompanied by economic gains in the portfolio exercise. A long--short strategy based on stocks' exposures to DEL-based inflation innovations delivers the highest annualized return and Sharpe ratio among the competing methods.

detail.abstract: Why do some centralized states keep official tax rates low? We model state building as a finite Markov decision process in which a ruler chooses centralization, taxation, and public goods under rebellion and invasion risks, solved by Q-learning, a reinforcement-learning algorithm converging to the dynamic-programming optimum. Optimal policy is non-monotone: centralization first raises fiscal capacity, then, by weakening elite compliance, leads the ruler to lower official taxation, creating a fiscal-capacity trap, with a parallel territory trap. We test the fiscal-capacity trap against the historical record of Japan, where official extraction follows the predicted inverted-U across regimes.

detail.abstract: This paper specifies a Layer-1 blockchain protocol whose monetary issuance is mechanically indexed to the network's verifiable operating cost plus a small, bounded margin. New tokens are minted only to the extent required to cover attested energy, compute, and infrastructure expenditure incurred in processing and finalizing blocks, and to fund a stability buffer. The design objective is a cryptoasset whose issuance adjusts to verified operating cost and prevailing token value, limiting cumulative dilution and dampening price volatility over time without reliance on fiat reserves. This revision incorporates a significant development in market infrastructure: the emergence of independent GPU rental-rate benchmarks and exchange-listed compute derivatives, which supply the protocol with regulated, market-settled reference rates for its cost oracle and permit hedging of the protocol's cost base. We present the issuance rule, admissible cost basis, attestation architecture, oracle design, fee and buffer mechanics, consensus model, threat model, governance, and institutional use cases for real-world-asset (RWA) tokenization and settlement.

This research investigates the deployment of Monolith, an applied artificial intelligence system combining tabular gradient boosting (CatBoost) and foundational time-series architectures (Chronos) delivered via a lightweight web-native platform. detail.abstract: This study examines how issues across boundaries influence contention dynamics in a movement of movements on social media. Participants utilize social media to support or oppose goals and actions related to their visions regarding societal changes. As the boundaries of movements are fluid on social media, we investigate the actors' identities, issues, and activities and how they interact with each other. We extend information systems theories of boundary spanning and conflict dynamics in social media and social movements literature to further understand how issues within and across boundaries influence contention dynamics in a movement of movements. We employed iterative qualitative and quantitative analyses using the computational theory construction approach to analyse social media messages from Twitter (now X) during a climate movement of movements. We identified key themes related to contention dynamics to understand how social media participants may collaborate or dispute with each other in movement of movements. Our model reveals the evolution of social media-enabled association and contention dynamics of movement of movements and how the ideological differences arise when negotiation influences digital activism for climaterelated goals and resolutions. This paper contributes to the understanding of how issues spanning specific social movements can lead to both conflicts and synergies in a movement of movements.

detail.abstract: We develop a joint backtesting framework for systemic risk measures (SRMs), including the Marginal Expected Shortfall (MES), Conditional Value-at-Risk (CoVaR), and Delta Conditional Value-at-Risk (∆CoVaR). Building on joint identification, we construct a general multivariate statistic that jointly assesses each SRM together with the risk measures required for its identification. We develop unconditional and conditional coverage tests for SRM forecasts accounting for parameter estimation risk. Monte Carlo simulations show competitive finite-sample power against a range of misspecifications, while the adjustment for estimation risk delivers good finite-sample size control. In an application to 93 large U.S. financial institutions over 2000-2023, using forecasts generated from a bivariate GARCH model with dynamic correlations, rejections of forecast validity cluster around the subprime crisis for all three SRMs, while CoVaR and ∆CoVaR exhibit additional rejection episodes, with the highest rejection rates for ∆CoVaR.

detail.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is an epistemic technology that produces propositions and reconfigures how organizations generate, validate, and retain what they treat as true. Its risks arise in human-GenAI dyadic interaction, where outputs can be miscategorized as warranted knowledge before responsibility for them is established, and in the wider organizational knowledge system, where miscategorized claims travel, accumulate authority, and reshape institutional memory. Using the principles of epistemic networks (epinets) and GenAI-supported strategic planning as an illustrative case, we explain how dyadic and network risks combine to threaten the integrity of organizational knowledge for four GenAI-enabled work modes: authenticated, automated, augmented, and autonomous. Following a diagnostic-design sequence, we then derive levers for stewarding the epistemic infrastructure (i.e., the socio-technical system of practices, technologies, and organizational structures) so that GenAI's role in organizational knowing is earned, qualified, and amenable to correction.

title: Beyond Rule Following: The Conscience Ensemble Model for Normatively Mature AI

detail.title: Beyond Rule Following: The Conscience Ensemble Model for Normatively Mature AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No financial Interest
declarations.funderStatement: Nobody

detail.abstract: Current AI alignment methods constrain behavior, specify principles, aggregate preferences, or evaluate outputs. We address a complementary architectural question: when may an input influence a judgment, and when is it authorized to modify the persistent state from which future judgments are made? The Conscience Ensemble Model (CEM) treats a functional analogue of conscience as an ensemble of relatively stable normative and epistemic perspectives dynamically orchestrated by a persistent artificial subject. Its central proposal is a separation between influence and update authority. Context may affect current deliberation without thereby acquiring the right to rewrite empirical beliefs or consolidated normative orientation. Normative-state change is modeled as a provenance-preserving and contestable process: proposal → challenge → authorization → commitment. No component that proposes a normative update may unilaterally authorize and commit it. In the initial prototype, authorization remains human. The artificial subject may nevertheless issue a reasoned remonstration. If disagreement remains unresolved, the authorized normative state remains operative while the alternative evaluation is retained in a Persistent Dissent Register inside the same persistent subject. The register has no action authority. A separate, temporary Dissent Evaluation procedure can later re-instantiate the recorded minority normative position on controlled probes using the same model and current factual state. This is not a second subject and not a counterfactual world simulation. We operationalize normative drift using explicitly logged orchestration allocations, a fixed probe suite, Jensen–Shannon distance with base-2 logarithms, and a test–retest noise floor. Dissent Evaluation adds a fidelity gate with its own re-instantiation noise floor: a recorded dissent state must reproduce its original evaluation, reasons, and orchestration anchors before longitudinal results are interpreted. This supports falsifiable tests of pressure versus reasons, semantic and provenance duplication, authorization quality, remonstration calibration, and reason-sensitive persistence or revision of unresolved normative dissent. CEM is not a complete theory of artificial Mündigkeit. It is proposed as one potentially necessary component in a broader architecture involving persistent subjecthood, epistemic competence, retrospective self-criticism, education, and governance.

title: A Dual Pathway Model of How Generative AI Use Shapes Creative Outcomes: Empirical Evidence from Human Representations in Artworks

detail.title: A Dual Pathway Model of How Generative AI Use Shapes Creative Outcomes: Empirical Evidence from Human Representations in Artworks
