detail.title: Evolution of Keynesianism and U.S. Economic Transformation: Toward a Structural Keynesianism for a Globalized and Digitized Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest regarding the research reported in this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: No financial support was received from public, commercial, or nonprofit funding agencies.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a historically grounded reinterpretation of Keynesianism in relation to U.S. economic transformation and the changing institutional structure of global capitalism. It traces Keynesian thought from Keynes's critique of self-adjusting markets through the IS-LM and aggregate demand-aggregate supply frameworks, disequilibrium and coordination-failure analysis, and subsequent debates involving monetarism, rational expectations, real business cycle theory, New Keynesian economics, Post-Keynesianism, institutional economics, and computational macroeconomics. Rather than presenting these developments as a succession of mutually exclusive doctrines, the paper shows how theoretical criticism, model building, empirical inquiry, and policy failure progressively expanded macroeconomics' understanding of demand, expectations, information, finance, distribution, incentives, and institutional adjustment. The paper argues that Keynesianism has endured because its central insight-that capitalist economies do not reliably generate full employment or stability through decentralized adjustment alone-has repeatedly proved relevant under changing historical conditions. The Great Depression, stagflation, the 2008 financial crisis, and the COVID-19 pandemic demonstrate, however, that instability cannot be explained or addressed through deficient aggregate demand alone. Real and supply shocks, financial fragility, productive constraints, public-health emergencies, regulatory failures, and inadequate administrative capacity can interact with declining expenditure to produce cumulative crises. The analysis accordingly interprets capitalism as an adaptive but fragile institutional order constituted through law, finance, corporations, labor relations, technology, political authority, and international arrangements. It examines how financialization, market concentration, rent extraction, inequality, fiscal commitments, global capital flows, dollarcentered monetary relations, deindustrialization, and regulatory capture shape macroeconomic performance and the transmission of policy. It further considers how international economic networks can become instruments of geopolitical coercion. Digital platforms and artificial intelligence intensify these structural problems by reorganizing corporate valuation, credit allocation, labor management, market access, data control, technological development, public administration, and the informational environment in which choices are formed. Platform gatekeeping and opaque algorithmic personalization may narrow effective choice, facilitate manipulation, and concentrate private authority over economic participation and democratic deliberation. In response, the paper develops a structural Keynesianism for a globalized, financialized, and AI-driven economy. This framework integrates demand management with financial regulation, competition policy, corporate-governance reform, labor institutions, industrial and technological strategy, public-sector capability, democratic accountability, and international coordination. It interprets crises not merely as temporary deviations from equilibrium but as possible manifestations of deeper misalignments among finance, production, technology, distribution, regulation, and political power. Structural Keynesianism is presented not as a fixed doctrine but as an empirically corrigible, computationally informed, and institutionally adaptive framework for democratic economic governance. Its purpose is to stabilize demand while reconstructing the institutional channels through which finance, public expenditure, and technological innovation become productive investment, secure employment, social capability, and broadly shared prosperity. In this mature form, Keynesianism offers a framework for reconciling macroeconomic stability and innovation with resilience, public purpose, effective freedom, and democratic self-government.

detail.abstract: Employment outcomes remain markedly unequal for autistic and other neurodivergent people. The proportion of autistic adults in employment rose from 16% in 2007 to 22% in 2016, but subsequently remained at about 22%, compared with 52% of disabled people and 81% of non-disabled people. These figures do not describe the type, pattern, or duration of employment (The Autism Employment Gap, 2016; Outcomes for disabled people in the UK, Office for National Statistics, 2021). Autistic candidates may encounter internal and external barriers when searching for, applying for, and securing work. Differences in social communication, information processing, and sensory experience can make lengthy or ambiguous job descriptions and interview questions particularly demanding. These barriers begin at the job-description stage; clearer and more accessible recruitment materials may enable employers to attract a wider range of capable candidates. This paper introduces three complementary frameworks designed to support employers and candidates across the recruitment cycle: the "Larkworthy-8 Stages of R", the "Accessibility Matrix", and the "Interviewing Strategies Matrix". The frameworks provide structured ways to review job descriptions, consider accessibility, discuss voluntary disclosure, and plan reasonable adjustments. Suggested practices include using clearer language, providing interview questions in advance, offering questions in alternative formats, and adapting interview arrangements to candidates' needs. Where candidates choose to disclose a health condition or disability, employers can use that information to discuss appropriate support; however, disclosure should remain voluntary and should not determine a candidate's suitability for the role. Together, the frameworks offer practical tools for reflecting on and improving equality, diversity, and inclusion throughout recruitment. They encourage Human Resource Management and Human Resource Development practitioners to reconsider established processes, reduce avoidable barriers, and assess candidates more consistently against the requirements of the role. Further evaluation is needed, but these frameworks may help employers create more accessible recruitment practices and improve employment opportunities for autistic and other neurodivergent candidates.

title: Systemic Fatigue as an Omitted Variable in African Economic Measurement: A Conceptual Framework and Research Agenda

detail.title: Systemic Fatigue as an Omitted Variable in African Economic Measurement: A Conceptual Framework and Research Agenda

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Interaction with Claude AI is acknowledged, but the author drove the whole process.
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded

detail.abstract: Official economic statistics for Sub-Saharan Africa are compiled under data-collection conditions that differ systematically from those in most other developing regions: longer and more burdensome household surveys, sparser administrative records, a very large informal sector, and recurring fiscal crises that strain the statistical agencies themselves. This paper argues that these conditions are not merely a source of random noise but a set of correlated, directional measurement biases-here grouped under the label systemic fatigue-that plausibly cause official statistics to understate African economic activity relative to other developing regions. We review the empirical literature on respondent and enumerator fatigue in African household surveys, summarize known measurement gaps arising from informality and fiscal stress, and propose an omitted-variable framework for testing whether fatigue proxies absorb part of the apparent Africa/non-Africa performance gap in standard growth and fiscal models. We specify a three-way comparative test, a candidate set of measurable proxies, an identification strategy, and the data sources needed to implement it. We are explicit throughout that the framework is a proposal : it has not yet been estimated, and the paper's contribution is to motivate and pre-specify the test-including its falsification condition-rather than to report a result.

detail.abstract: The Securities Law 2006 established the legal framework governing the securities market in Vietnam-the Securities Law 2019 later replaced it. In 2009, amendments to the Penal Code introduced three new provisions for securities fraud-intentional disclosure of false information, insider trading and market manipulation. These amendments marked the first prohibition of securities fraud under the Penal Code since the stock market opened in 2000. The provisions of the Penal Code were rarely used until the Chairman of FLC Group was arrested on 29 March 2022 for stock market manipulation. The event highlighted problems with the current legal framework governing securities fraud in Vietnam. This article examines the incidence of securities fraud in Vietnam, analyses key unreported cases and considers reasons why it is difficult to prosecute securities fraud, notwithstanding the provisions of Chs VIII and IX of the Securities Law 2019, which came into force on 1 January 2021.

title: The Unemployment-Inflation Trade-off After COVID-19: Evidence from a State-Level Panel of Indian States (2012-2024)

detail.title: The Unemployment-Inflation Trade-off After COVID-19: Evidence from a State-Level Panel of Indian States (2012-2024)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research used no external funding.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether the COVID-19 pandemic induced an unemployment-inflation slope shift in the Phillips curve across Indian states. Using an annual panel of 29 states and union territories spanning from 2012 to 2024, we estimate four progressively augmented specifications - a baseline, an expectations-augmented, a New Keynesian, and a structural break model. The models jointly test for cross-sectional dependence, slope heterogeneity, and a COVID-induced shift in the unemployment-inflation slope. Diagnostic tests reveal pervasive cross-sectional dependence (Pesaran CD statistics of 15-40 on fixed-effects residuals) and statistically significant slope heterogeneity, invalidating standard pooled and fixed-effects estimators and motivating the use of the Common Correlated Effects Mean Group (CCEMG) estimator as the primary specification. The focal model reveals that the pre-COVID unemployment-inflation slope is conventionally negative (-0.567), while the interaction between unemployment and a post-COVID indicator is positive and statistically significant (2.552, p = 0.033). This implies a post-COVID slope of 1.985, which is a reversal in sign rather than a mere flattening or steepening. This structural break is corroborated by a Chow test (F = 11.446, p < 0.001) and is robust across 28 of 29 states in a jackknife analysis, with Nagaland identified as the sole high-leverage exception. The findings suggest that the pandemic fundamentally altered the inflation-generating process in India, with implications for the conduct of monetary policy under the Reserve Bank of India's flexible inflation-targeting framework.

detail.abstract: New technologies swept through Britain during the Second Industrial Revolution, destroying old jobs and creating new ones. We know little about how workers reallocated. Using 170 million full-count British census observations (1851-1911), I construct new task-level data on occupation and investigate English bootmaking as it mechanized. 153,000 artisanal jobs disappeared as skills became obsolete; 140,000 specialized jobs emerged. Incumbent artisans did not take the new jobs, nor were they displaced. Instead, entry collapsed-young men stopped entering the old trade. New jobs went primarily to young workers, though not in the same locations. Young cohorts absorbed the adjustment.

detail.abstract: Using a time-varying vector autoregressive model, we analyze daily return predictability of U.S.-dollar-hedged global green and conventional bond indices. Long-run return predictability rises slightly after the Paris Agreement for the two bond markets as a whole and, in particular, in the component of returns that moves jointly across the two markets. It rises more sharply during the COVID-19 period and declines afterward. By contrast, the relative return between green and conventional bonds shows no comparable pattern. We interpret these findings using a two-bond asset pricing model of beauty contests. The Paris Agreement provides an imprecise public signal about a small latent change in institutional participation; later public evidence gradually aligns beliefs, and persistent institutional rebalancing interacts with resale-price expectations. Positive payoff covariance gives a green-originating order a larger common-return loading than green-relative loading. The response is initially weak and gradually strengthens. Normalized calculations illustrate this mechanism. A separate extension shows that lower intermediary risk tolerance can amplify an existing response during later stress.

detail.abstract: Fixed costs account for an increasing share of operating expenses in the U.S. banking system. From 1995 to 2026, estimated fixed costs rose from 37 percent to 62 percent as a share of total noninterest expense. Over the same period, estimated marginal and average operating costs declined, loan spreads and net interest margins fell, and estimated loan markups increased by 21 percentage points. These trends are pervasive across banks but are most pronounced among large banks. We develop a model of bank industry dynamics with endogenous fixed costs to rationalize these long-run trends and examine pro-competitive effects. While competition increases credit supply, it decreases lending efficiency and increases bank risk-taking.

detail.abstract: Purpose-Most large organisations now use AI at work, and most users say it saves them time. Yet the share of organisations reporting any effect on profit has not moved in a year. This paper asks what the evidence supports about 2027, where the current HR model is losing money and manager time, and which changes in priority-setting would recover them. Design/methodology/approach-An evidence synthesis of 47 industry, official and legal sources published between January 2025 and August 2026, graded by design, and 15 peer-reviewed studies, including four field experiments and three meta-analyses. Claims about direction rest on several sources; each magnitude is tied to one named study. Findings-The gap between individual and enterprise returns from AI is explained by a loop. Value needs work redesign. Redesign lands on managers whose spans have risen by about half since 2013, and they experience it as more change. How that change is handled sets the engagement that decides whether AI is used. Five propositions follow, each with evidence of need and evidence of effect. Practical implications-HR should set a span ceiling and a change ceiling before funding new programmes, plan work at task level over three years, and measure AI by redesigned workflows rather than licences. Originality/value-The paper treats the AI return gap as a manager-capacity problem rather than an adoption problem, ranks the leaks in the current HR model by cost, and states what would show it wrong.

detail.abstract: Echo chambers, social environments where like-minded individuals reinforce shared beliefs, have been extensively studied in political and public health contexts, yet their relevance for brands and consumer behavior remains unexplored. This paper explores echo chambers in a brand context and examines how consumers in brand echo chambers, i.e., surrounded by others with similar brand preferences, perceive and behave toward brands. It introduces two complementary measures of brand echo chambers using a large-scale dataset of over 870,000 X followers across 179 brands. The first measure reflects brand embeddedness among the focal social circle, while the second captures brand exclusivity within the same circle by identifying connections tied solely to the brand. We find that consumers in stronger brand echo chambers discuss brands more frequently and favorably, mention competitors less often, and exhibit stronger emotional engagement when discussing brands. These insights show that brands can leverage readily available social media data to derive echo-chamber metrics and track consumer networks and their relative exposure to the focal brand and competitors. These metrics can also serve as scalable segmentation and targeting signals by helping managers identify consumers whose network structures are associated with distinct patterns of brand and competitor related behavior.

title: Measuring Lost Futures: A Layered Reachability Model for Adaptive Systems

detail.title: Measuring Lost Futures: A Layered Reachability Model for Adaptive Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because this theoretical and computational study involved no human participants, patient data, animal subjects, clinical interventions, or personally identifiable information. The empirical component consists solely of a secondary analysis of previously published, aggregated, and publicly available data.

detail.abstract: A patient can return to a blood pressure of 120/80 after a haemorrhage while becoming less able to survive the next one. A factory can set a production record by consuming the reserve that would have kept it operating through winter. These cases expose the same measurement problem: the present state does not reveal the structure, cost, independence, or ownership of the system's remaining response paths. This article defines that hidden object as an architecture of possibility: the actor-specific, horizon-dependent structure of viable future configurations and the routes by which they remain reachable. Every transition carries non-commensurable time, capital, institutional, and epistemic resistance; hard feasibility conditions remain explicit gates; and reachability is computed component-wise under declared budgets. The same framework gives a functional definition of accessibility memory: history is active when it changes a later transition under matched present conditions. Three internal results connect the framework to measurement: represented reachability is monotone under edge addition and component-wise cost reduction; current-state variables cannot identify different conditional responses when state-matched systems retain different feasible paths; and multidimensional possibility profiles admit no complete ranking without declared values. A reproducible eight-node model shows equal current output with sharply different post-shock reachability. In a structurally nested family of 6,000 parameterizations, the option-preserving regime strictly dominates after shock in 96.3 percent of runs and ties in the remainder; this establishes computability and within-family robustness, rather than an empirical frequency. In a separate held-out benchmark of 6,000 synthetic histories, a fixed layered-reachability model distinguishes post-shock outcomes that a current-state specification cannot recover. Because the generator is topology-dependent and the state-only comparator contains no topological variables, the comparison demonstrates internal predictive discrimination, not external validation. Explicit accessibility-memory covariates produce no reliable additional reduction in primary-outcome error once current reachability is observed. A Dutch Rhine reanalysis, a prospective 2026-2031 protocol, and explicit rejection criteria turn these distinctions into a falsifiable research programme.

detail.abstract: For a connected simple graph G, let c(G) = |E(G)|-|V (G)| + 1 and let s(L(G)) denote the positive minus negative adjacency inertia of its line graph. We certify that 2s(L(G)) ≤ c(G) + 1 for every graph G of order nine. The verification exhausts all 261,080 connected isomorphism classes and uses exact rational congruence, with an independent verification by integer characteristic polynomials and Sturm root counts. There are six equality classes, all unicyclic, and the inequality is strict on the other 261,074 classes. This is a finite result; the universal inequality remains open.

title: The Rhythm of Resilience: What Hindustani Classical Music, Taal and Tabla Teach Us About Organisational Resilience

detail.title: The Rhythm of Resilience: What Hindustani Classical Music, Taal and Tabla Teach Us About Organisational Resilience

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No personal or financial relationship with other people or organizations
declarations.funderStatement: Not applicable

detail.abstract: Research on organisational resilience has borrowed its central ideas primarily from ecology and psychology. In each of those fields, the thing studied either has no intentions of its own or is a single person. An organisation is neither. It is a purposeful collective that must pass on knowhow across generations, coordinate expert work in real time, and hold on to an identity while changing what it does. While several living artistic traditions demonstrate these properties, jazz has been the primary source to draw parallels to organisational creativity, improvisation, and flexibility-constructs that arguably are subsets of resilience and do not explain resilience holistically. To gain broader insights into resilience, I use analogical reasoning to examine Hindustani classical music, a tradition that has survived dynastic collapse, colonial rule, the loss of courtly patronage, waves of technological disruption, and repeated displacement of its own dominant forms, and has emerged stronger and more resourceful. I analyse it as two coupled subsystems, raag (melody) and taal (rhythm and time), and examine taal through its principal instrument, the tabla. Drawing on ethnomusicological literature, acoustic and neurocognitive evidence, and practitioner knowledge, I identify ten mechanisms and consolidate them into the Taal Framework for organisational resilience, which has five design domains arranged in order of dependency: instrumentation, architecture, capability, coordination and renewal. The central finding is that resilience comes from pairing a small, rigid deep structure with wide freedom at the surface. I call this 'generative constraint'. Two cases show that systemic resilience is necessary but not sufficient; individual agency is what activates it. The paper, by adopting a novel analogical base, contributes broader insights to organisational resilience theory and provides directions for future empirical research.

title: The Dark Knight Paradox: Why Corrective Disruption is Perceived as Destructive Disruption
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Dark Knight Paradox: Why Corrective Disruption is Perceived as Destructive Disruption

The author is also involved in an ongoing employment-related legal dispute with that organization. These relationships may reasonably be perceived as relevant to the interpretation of the case. detail.abstract:
This paper proposes the Dark Knight Paradox as a theoretical framework for explaining why organizational actors who seek to correct dysfunction may come to be perceived as threats to the very order they intend to improve. Research on employee voice, organizational silence, psychological safety, challenging voice, threat-rigidity, whistleblowing, constructive deviance, and institutional work has shown that even potentially beneficial dissent may be interpreted by managers as threatening, disloyal, or disruptive. Yet less attention has been given to the process through which disruption intended to repair an organization becomes perceptually reclassified as disruption intended to damage it.

The paper defines Corrective Disruption as an intervention that temporarily destabilizes existing arrangements in order to restore or improve their long-term functionality, safety, learning capacity, fairness, or capacity for dialogue. It then introduces Corrective–Destructive Perceptual Inversion to describe the process through which such intervention is interpreted by defenders of the existing order as destructive disruption because it unsettles established authority, roles, legitimacy, evaluations, or procedural stability. Batman and Joker are used only as analytical metaphors rather than personality types. Accordingly, Jokerization does not mean that a corrective actor becomes destructive; it refers to the social attribution of destructive intent to an actor whose intervention may have been corrective in purpose.

The model connects problem recognition, corrective disruption, threat perception, shifts of attention from the issue to the problem-raiser, perceptual inversion, institutional defense, and subsequent marginalization or repair. It further proposes the Self-Obsolescence Principle: corrective intervention reaches its strongest form of success when the underlying problem improves and the organization can sustain that improvement without continued intervention by the original problem-raiser. From this perspective, organizational maturity does not require the absence of threat perceptions. Rather, it requires the capacity to reconsider threat classifications, separate the evaluation of a claim from the evaluation of its claimant, and terminate defensive responses when they are no longer necessary.

The Dark Knight Paradox therefore offers a middle-range theory linking employee voice, organizational defense, constructive deviance, institutional change, and post-conflict repair. Its central claim is that the same disruptive act may be understood as corrective or destructive depending on the observer’s position within the order being challenged.

title: Beyond Physical Safety: Psychological First Aid in Disaster Response and Recovery

detail.title: Beyond Physical Safety: Psychological First Aid in Disaster Response and Recovery

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

declarations.funderStatement: This work received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Disasters create consequences that extend beyond immediate physical danger. Survivors may face uncertainty, displacement, disrupted routines, separation from social supports, urgent practical needs, and psychological distress while simultaneously attempting to navigate unfamiliar response and recovery systems. Psychological First Aid (PFA) provides an evidence-informed framework for supporting individuals after disasters through practical assistance, safety and stabilization, connection with social supports, information, coping assistance, and linkage with needed services. This white paper examines the role of PFA within disaster response and recovery, with particular attention to survivor safety, connection, agency, practical support, and the transition from immediate response into longer-term recovery. It considers how emergency managers, public-safety professionals, responders, volunteers, healthcare personnel, community organizations, and other disaster-support partners can apply PFA principles without exceeding appropriate professional boundaries or representing PFA as psychotherapy or clinical treatment. The analysis emphasizes that psychological support should be integrated with, rather than separated from, the practical and operational dimensions of disaster assistance. It further examines organizational readiness, responder communication, survivor autonomy, cultural and contextual considerations, referral pathways, and the importance of evidence-informed implementation. The paper argues that effective disaster support requires more than restoring physical safety alone; it requires systems capable of recognizing and responding to the psychological and social consequences that influence how individuals experience and navigate recovery. PFA therefore represents one component of a broader disaster-support continuum designed to promote humane, practical, survivor-centered assistance while connecting individuals with additional services when needs exceed the scope of immediate supportive intervention.

detail.abstract: This study examines St. John Bosco’s early experience of displacement and manual labor at the Moglia farm (1826–1828) as a foundational inspiration to the Salesian mission for migrant youth. Set against the socio-economic turbulence of post-Napoleonic 19th-century Italy—characterized by rural poverty, agrarian child labor, and urban migration—this paper analyzes young John's two-year tenure as a hired hand. By synthesizing historical sources and Salesian hagiography, the article extracts the theological, pedagogical, and pastoral implications of Don Bosco's Moglia Farm experience.

detail.title: Estimating Hierarchical Demand in Retail Operations

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Operations Management  [10.1002/joom.70058]

detail.abstract: A hierarchical structure over product attributes is a central input to many product assortment and inventory optimization models, yet no existing method can recover such structures from the aggregate sales data that retailers routinely collect. We introduce HASTERAD (hierarchical attribute substitution tree estimation via recursive attribute discovery), which recovers a substitution tree from standard SKU-store-week scanner data. Leveraging variation in prices and promotions, HASTERAD compares attribute-based substitution patterns and then recursively partitions the product space to recover a candidate hierarchy of attribute-level substitution. Applied to the IRI Marketing Data Set, it recovers a stable and economically interpretable tree. To quantify its economic value, we execute a three-step optimization process on synthetic data with known ground truth: we recover a tree with HASTERAD, estimate demand parameters on that tree, and optimize assortments. HASTERAD's chosen assortments forgo less than 11% of the profit available to a clairvoyant planner, even in demanding settings where a traditional flat demand model forgoes almost 100%. Performance remains strong whether the method is applied to a multi-store panel, where stockouts are unobservable, or to a single store's internal records, where data are sparse but stockouts are observed. These findings are robust across several alternative specifications. Our central empirical finding concerns model selection. A tree chosen by best in-sample fit, from an exhaustive search over simple hierarchies, fits the observed sales nearly as well as HASTERAD's recovered tree, yet prescribes assortments whose expected profits are substantially lower. Fit evaluates observed purchases, but assortment optimization depends on predicting demand under assortments not yet observed.

title: Digital Oversight and Administrative Discretion: A Theoretical Framework and Research Agenda for Street-Level Bureaucracy

detail.title: Digital Oversight and Administrative Discretion: A Theoretical Framework and Research Agenda for Street-Level Bureaucracy

detail.abstract: Modern e-governance platforms that aim to strengthen public accountability often mandate strict procedural regulations and automated audit trails, with the intention of curbing widespread corruption. However, aggressive digital oversight risks fostering a hyper-procedural system-level bureaucracy. Integrating street-level bureaucracy theory with Edmondson’s psychological safety framework, this study proposes a theoretical framework to investigate how continuous digital monitoring reshapes decision-making among frontline bureaucrats. Using a mixed-methods research design, the framework identifies felt interpersonal risk as a critical mechanism driving frontline officers towards defensive rule following and informal workarounds. Additionally, it examines whether in-service capacity building programs moderate the psychological anxiety felt by frontline bureaucrats. By illuminating the human behavioural dynamics underlying the state digital infrastructure, this study proposes to offer evidence-based insights to help design digital public infrastructure that harmonises digital transparency with protected administrative discretion and the psychological safety of bureaucrats. Consequently, this ensures that compliance protocols do not compromise citizen-centric service delivery.

title: Stockouts, Pageviews, and Data Imputation: Implications for Managing Long-tail Products
affiliations: Beijing Jiaotong University - School of Economics and Management , Rotman School of Management, JD.com Smart Supply Chain Y, JD.com Smart Supply Chain Y, JD.com Smart Supply Chain Y and JD.com Smart Supply Chain Y

detail.title: Stockouts, Pageviews, and Data Imputation: Implications for Managing Long-tail Products

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no
declarations.funderStatement: no

detail.abstract: Long-tail products are prevalent on e-commerce platforms and are plagued by stockouts and censored demand data. To infer demand and build prediction models, retailers may rely on pageviews and other visibility measures as proxies. However, stockouts can distort these proxies, leading to biased training data and poor forecasts. How can retailers effectively impute these affected signals to improve demand prediction for the long tail? Methodology/results: We first empirically analyze how stockouts affect realized pageviews using three large long-tail data sets from JD.com: based on matching and robust synthetic control (RSC) designs, we show pageviews fall significantly following stockout onset across the product categories. We then propose a data-imputation framework, informed by the counterfactual analysis, that estimates the pageview paths that would have been observed had an SKU remained in stock and uses these paths to construct improved sales labels for demand forecasting. We construct these paths using Matching and RSC and further develop a Hybrid Matching-RSC approach that uses Matching to select comparable SKUs before applying RSC to their pageview histories. Through a large-scale rollinghorizon experiment, we show that all three implementations of the framework improve forecasting accuracy. Hybrid method performs the best, reducing out-of-sample wMAPE by 16.78%-27.28% across the product categories. Managerial implications: Product pageviews are valuable demand signals, but they can be distorted when stockouts affect how SKUs are displayed and viewed on a platform. Our imputation and forecasting framework helps mitigate this distortion, improve demand forecasts, and enable better-informed replenishment decisions for long-tail products.

title: Human-AI Collaborative Decision-Making for Risk Management and Adaptive Digital Environments
affiliations: University of Zurich

detail.title: Human-AI Collaborative Decision-Making for Risk Management and Adaptive Digital Environments

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I am the sole author of this research paper and declare that I have no known financial or personal relationships that could have influenced the research or its conclusions.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this research because it did not involve human participants, patients, or the collection of personal or sensitive data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Organizations are increasingly deploying artificial intelligence to support risk-related decision-making in adaptive digital environments, yet purely automated risk scoring risks either over-reliance in ambiguous situations or the erosion of human contextual judgment, while purely human risk assessment is constrained by bounded attention and inconsistent, bias-prone heuristics. Building on an automated riskassessment and collaborative decision-making framework developed for agile project management and stakeholder engagement, this study generalizes that framework into a domain-agnostic human-AI collaborative decision architecture for risk management, and evaluates it through a disclosed synthetic proof-of-concept. Three formal research questions are addressed: whether AI-only risk classification significantly outperforms bounded human judgment (RQ1), whether a confidence-gated collaborative delegation policy significantly reduces the critical-risk miss rate relative to AI-only (RQ2), and what the quantified, statistically grounded accuracy cost of that policy is (RQ3). Using a literature-informed synthetic dataset of 10,000 risk-assessment events spanning four severity classes (Low, Medium, High, Critical), three decision configurations, an AI-only Random Forest classifier, a simulated human-only heuristic, and a trust-calibrated human-AI collaborative configuration were evaluated on an illustrative held-out split and, to test the study's hypotheses rigorously, across 30 independently resampled train/test trials with paired statistical testing and a fixed delegation threshold. The AI-only configuration was significantly more accurate than the human-only heuristic across all 30 trials (mean 87.9% versus 63.3%, paired t-test p < .0001, Cohen's d = 31.9), confirming H1. Consistent with the single-split illustration, the collaborative configuration's accuracy was significantly lower than AI-only's across trials (mean 86.5% versus 87.9%, p < .0001, Cohen's d =-3.42), confirming H3. However, the rigorous 30-trial validation did not confirm H2: rather than reducing the critical-risk miss rate as the single illustrative split suggested (6.6% versus 7.7%), the collaborative configuration's critical-risk miss rate was in fact significantly higher The study contributes a generalized, reusable human-AI collaborative decision architecture, a reproducible statistical-validation methodology, and transparent, hypothesis-tested evidence including a disconfirmed hypothesis about when collaborative delegation helps and when it does not. Limitations, theoretical and practical implications, and directions for validation on real organizational data are discussed.

title: Discretionary Voids: An Institutional Design Theory of Authorized Action
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Discretionary Voids: An Institutional Design Theory of Authorized Action

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Discretion is central to public administration, law, and organizational theory. Yet the literature has left a foundational question unasked: what are the factual conditions under which discretion is authorized to act? Existing frameworks authorize action without specifying its triggers, producing what this paper terms discretionary voids-institutional spaces in which authorization exists but its activation conditions remain unspecified. The consequence is a legitimacy deficit: authorized action rests on unrecoverable subjective states rather than auditable factual criteria. This paper offers an institutional design theory to fill such voids. It introduces three constitutive elements of a complete authorization design: discretionary rules linking observable facts to action boundaries; inviolable boundaries establishing ex-ante prohibitions; and ex-post auditability as a design criterion for institutional accountability. The theory is developed and illustrated through use-offorce decisions, which serve as the extreme case for the framework-not because the theory is limited to this domain, but because the stakes are highest, the costs of ambiguity most severe, and the theoretical gap most visible. The resulting logic is generalizable to any domain where authorized action requires trigger conditions: administrative enforcement, regulatory intervention, medical authorization, and beyond.

title: Periodic Vehicle Routing for Food Bank Distribution with Workload Equity and Schedule Persistence
affiliations: , State University of New York (SUNY) - University at Buffalo, University at Buffalo, State University of New York (SUNY) - University at Buffalo and  Universidad de La Sabana

detail.title: Periodic Vehicle Routing for Food Bank Distribution with Workload Equity and Schedule Persistence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding.

detail.abstract: Food insecurity affects millions worldwide, and food banks that distribute donated food to networks of partner agencies face a recurring operational problem: scheduling agencies with heterogeneous visit frequencies and routing a limited vehicle fleet while keeping driver workloads equitable and preserving the stability of established schedules. We formalize this as a periodic heterogeneous vehicle routing problem with workload-equity and schedule-persistence requirements and develop a solution framework for it. We present four contributions. First, we formulate an integer linear program unifying agency-to-day assignment and vehicle routing, incorporating heterogeneous delivery frequencies, compatibility requirements, time window constraints, and bi-objective optimization balancing routing efficiency against workload equity. Second, we develop a sequential decomposition strategy that restores tractability at operational scale, and we validate it empirically against a balance-constrained exact benchmark, quantifying the optimality cost of decomposition. Third, we introduce a persistence-constrained extension generating assignments with controlled deviation from existing operations, enabling incremental improvement while maintaining organizational stability. Fourth, we develop an integrated tabu search metaheuristic for rapid replanning scenarios. We instantiate the framework on Banco de Alimentos de Bogotá (BdA), a Colombian food bank serving over 500,000 people through more than 450 partner agencies, and benchmark it against routing-only and assignment-only baselines. The sequential approach achieves near-perfect weekly balance while generating implementable routes whose median vehicle workload imbalance is a quarter of a minute; the decomposition is provably optimal on a third of validation instances (median optimality gap 6.6\% otherwise). The persistence framework achieves a 95\% reduction in daily demand imbalance (over 99\% weekly) by modifying assignments for only 20\% of agencies, and the heuristic delivers comparable routing quality substantially faster.

title: Who Moderates the Moderator?
affiliations: Independent Scholar

detail.title: Who Moderates the Moderator?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial relationship with Boris Barbour, the PubPeer Foundation, PubPeer, Peeriodicals, Referee #3, any Foundation customer or donor, or any researcher whose work has been discussed on PubPeer.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this article.

detail.abstract: Boris Barbour is a neuroscientist, PubPeer co-organizer and board member of the PubPeer Foundation. He has also served as the Foundation’s treasurer and as a public advocate for anonymous post-publication review. This article does not challenge the legitimacy of correcting scientific errors or protecting vulnerable critics. It examines whether PubPeer’s governance has kept pace with the power Barbour and his colleagues have helped the platform acquire. The public record reveals a structural contradiction. PubPeer heavily moderates content but states that it does not scientifically review comments and provides no warranty of their truth. It encourages strong anonymity, cannot evaluate anonymous commenters’ motives or conflicts, requires authors to reply through signed institutionally validated accounts, and ordinarily retains criticism even after a convincing response or journal correction. Its terms reserve broad discretion, disclaim reputational harm and offer discontinuation of use as the remedy for dissatisfaction, although a criticized author cannot withdraw a public thread merely by leaving the platform. Meanwhile, the Foundation shares comment data through paid Dashboards, received a major institutional award, offers monthly cash prizes for selected comments and is now linked directly from Web of Science. Barbour’s personal Referee #3 blog adds a second accountability problem: categorical rhetoric and unannounced minor edits to public scientific criticism. None of this establishes that Barbour authored anonymous comments, manipulated a moderation decision, profited personally, harassed a researcher or committed misconduct. It does establish a need for named governance responsibility, published moderator standards, independent appeal, durable version histories, prominent resolution labels, incentive safeguards and annual outcome reporting.
